<!-- ============ INTRO ============ -->
<header class="rs-intro">
  <h1 class="rs-title">Research</h1>
  <p class="rs-lede">From Appalachian creeks to coral reefs, I study how animals move, feed, and recycle nutrients, and how global change is reshaping all three. Explore where the work happens, then read what we found.</p>
</header>

<!-- ============ MAP ============ -->
<!-- Sites are listed in the SITES array in the script at the bottom of this page.

<!-- ============ THEMES ============ -->
<section class="rs-theme" id="movement">
  <figure class="rs-theme-photo">
    <img src="images/web/fiu-snook-workup.jpg" alt="Mack preparing a Common Snook for acoustic tagging on a boat in the Shark River" loading="lazy">
    <figcaption>Acoustic tagging surgery on a Common Snook in Tarpon Bay, Everglades National Park</figcaption>
  </figure>
  <div class="rs-theme-text">
    <p class="rs-kicker" style="--c: var(--rs-move)">Animal movement</p>
    <h2>When, where, and why do animals move?</h2>
    <p>Using acoustic telemetry, accelerometers, and long-term tracking, I follow individual predators through the coastal Everglades to learn how temperature, water levels, and body size shape what they do.</p>
    <ul class="rs-findings">
      <li>Common Snook activity dropped sharply above 26&nbsp;°C, and fish switched between day and night activity at temperature extremes.
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.260735">White et al. 2026, <i>Royal Society Open Science</i></a></li>
      <li>In wetter years, individual snook specialized more in where they spent their time, and specialists ate a narrower range of prey.
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-82158-4">Santos et al. 2025, <i>Scientific Reports</i></a></li>
      <li>Most snook that left the Shark River did so in spawning season, and about half came back, showing one river is only part of their range.
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/mcfafs/vtaf050">Goldner et al. 2026, <i>Marine and Coastal Fisheries</i></a></li>
      <li>Spotted Seatrout in Florida Bay choose habitat at two scales at once: the seagrass patch and the wider seascape.
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-27322-0">Rodemann et al. 2025, <i>Scientific Reports</i></a></li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</section>

<section class="rs-theme rs-flip" id="nutrients">
  <figure class="rs-theme-photo">
    <img src="images/web/ttu-sucker-bank.jpg" alt="Mack holding a migrant Smallmouth Buffalo beside Citico Creek" loading="lazy">
    <figcaption>Migrant Smallmouth Buffalo sampled from Citico Creek, Cherokee National Forest</figcaption>
  </figure>
  <div class="rs-theme-text">
    <p class="rs-kicker" style="--c: var(--rs-nutr)">Nutrients and food webs</p>
    <h2>How do animals move nutrients and energy through ecosystems?</h2>
    <p>Fish recycle nutrients through excretion and carry them between habitats in their bodies and eggs. I measure those fluxes, from a single spawning run to decades of data across ocean ecosystems.</p>
    <ul class="rs-findings">
      <li>About 67,000 migrating Smallmouth Buffalo delivered an estimated 730&nbsp;kg of nitrogen and 80&nbsp;kg of phosphorus to Citico Creek in a single spawning season.
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/eff.12676">White et al. 2023, <i>Ecology of Freshwater Fish</i></a></li>
      <li>Migrating redhorses delivered a spring pulse of nitrogen, mostly through their eggs, when the stream was exporting little nitrogen of its own.
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/eff.12758">Hudson et al. 2024, <i>Ecology of Freshwater Fish</i></a></li>
      <li>Across ~25 years and ~1.5 million fishes in coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, and kelp forests, richer fish communities supplied nitrogen more steadily.
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2532469123">White et al. 2026, <i>PNAS</i></a></li>
      <li>In warmer water, snook ate fewer fish and more often had empty stomachs, meaning they must eat more low-quality prey to meet their energy needs.
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/mcfafs/vtaf031">White et al. 2025, <i>Marine and Coastal Fisheries</i></a></li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</section>

<section class="rs-theme" id="rivers">
  <figure class="rs-theme-photo">
    <img src="images/web/osu-gravel-bar.jpg" alt="View from a sampling boat of the Scioto River beside a gravel bar" loading="lazy">
    <figcaption>Lunch break on the Scioto River, OH</figcaption>
  </figure>
  <div class="rs-theme-text">
    <p class="rs-kicker" style="--c: var(--rs-river)">Rivers under global change</p>
    <h2>How do flow loss, warming, and invasions reshape river communities?</h2>
    <p>Rivers in the Colorado River basin are drying as demand for water grows, and Ohio's rivers face invasive carp and changing land use. I study what these pressures mean for native fishes and aquatic insects.</p>
    <ul class="rs-findings">
      <li>Across seven Colorado River basin rivers, aquatic insect communities were less diverse where flows have declined the most.
        <span class="rs-status">White et al., in review, <i>Ecohydrology</i></span></li>
      <li>In the White River, Utah, long considered a refuge, native fish densities declined from 2008 to 2025 while nonnative fishes stayed abundant.
        <span class="rs-status">Porter et al., in review, <i>Biological Conservation</i></span></li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</section>

  </ol>
</section>

<section class="rs-open">
  <div>
    <h2 class="rs-h3">Open data and code</h2>
    <p>Datasets I've published through the Environmental Data Initiative:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Nitrogen and phosphorus excretion rates of individual marine and estuarine animals (2025)</li>
      <li>Seasonal electrofishing data from Rookery Branch and Tarpon Bay, Everglades National Park, 2004 to present (2025)</li>
      <li>Movements of aquatic predators in the Shark River estuary, Everglades National Park, 2007 to present (2025)</li>
    </ul>
    <p class="rs-links"><a href="https://github.com/mackwhite">Code on GitHub</a> <a href="https://mackwhite.github.io/aquatic-ecology-osu/">Aquatic Ecology course site</a> <a href="CV.html#publications">All publications</a></p>
